title: A court of many faiths
hook: a Muslim foreign minister, Hindu and Dogra ministers, and European officers served at his court

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Koh-i-Noor, the mountain of light, and your line was what is precious. Did you give ten minutes to the thing you chose? Today, the people in the room where the diamond was shown. Day nine hundred twenty.

A foreign visitor at the Lahore court is shown in by a man in a Muslim scholar's dress, who speaks for the kingdom. Across the hall stand Hindu officials who keep the accounts, Dogra brothers from the hills who manage the Maharaja's household, Sikh generals with their turbans and swords, and a few officers in European coats who drill the army. All of them answer to one man. Today: a court of many faiths.
screen: `A MUSLIM SCHOLAR SPEAKS FOR LAHORE.` → `HINDU, DOGRA, SIKH, EUROPEAN.` → `ALL IN ONE HALL.`

segments.voice: Start with the man who spoke for the kingdom. Fakir Azizuddin was a Muslim, a physician and a scholar, and he served the Maharaja as his trusted adviser and envoy. When the British or the Afghans needed to hear from Lahore, he was often the one they heard. Histories remember his tact and his learning. Second, the ministers. The Dogra brothers, Gulab Singh and Dhian Singh among them, rose high at court, and Dhian Singh became chief minister. Hindu officials ran the treasury and the revenue, and Hindu commanders, like the general who took Kashmir, led armies. Third, the soldiers from far away. You've already met the European officers who trained the army. Some of them had served Napoleon, histories say, and they came to Lahore and stayed. And fourth, what holds it together. This was the Sarkar-e-Khalsa, the government in the Khalsa's name, with coins struck in the Gurus' names. Yet the people running it came from many faiths. Sikh tradition points back to the Gurus for the reason. In a hymn of Guru Arjan, the Guru says he is neither Hindu nor Muslim: his body and breath belong to the One whom Hindus call Ram and Muslims call Allah. A court of many faiths fits that old teaching. It wasn't perfect, and the ministers' rivalries will matter later in this story. But the Maharaja chose people for what they could do, and let them keep their own way of praying.
screen: `FAKIR AZIZUDDIN SPEAKS FOR LAHORE.` · `DOGRA AND HINDU MINISTERS.` · `OFFICERS FROM EUROPE.` · `A KHALSA STATE, MANY FAITHS IN IT.` · then, large: `MANY FAITHS, ONE COURT.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with the people you work beside. Sit, and let your breath slow. Bring to mind the people in your daily life who are different from you: different faith, background, age, or way of doing things. Picture them one by one. For each, name one thing they do well, something you'd want on your team. Let the list grow. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.

Fakir Azizuddin, the Muslim physician and envoy who spoke for Lahore, serving a court of many faiths: Dogra and Hindu ministers, Sikh generals and European officers, all serving one Khalsa kingdom. Today's word.
Your line: many faiths, one court. Today, work well with someone who isn't like you. Ask their view first, and use it. Day nine hundred twenty.

howItsDone: Sikhs often point to Maharaja Ranjit Singh's court, with its Muslim, Hindu, Dogra, Sikh and European officials, as an example of the Gurus' teaching of one Lord whom Hindus and Muslims each name in their own way.
